Segment Revenue: Global RIM vs Global Data Center

adjustedEbitdaMargin.title: Adjusted EBITDA margin
adjustedEbitdaMargin.content:
Adjusted EBITDA margin is management's non-GAAP EBITDA (adjusted for restructuring, transaction and other items) divided by revenue -- the company's preferred profitability gauge.

For Iron Mountain Incorporated: the mix shift toward Global Data Center, a higher-margin segment with heavier upfront capex, is management's stated path to margin expansion; FY2022-FY2025 rose from 35.8% to 37.3%.

What to watch:

  • Margin tracking the data-center revenue share
  • Gap to reported (GAAP) margin from the add-backs

dataCenterCapacity.title: Data center capacity
dataCenterCapacity.content:
Leasable capacity is contracted-and-built data-center megawatts generating revenue today; under development is MW committed to future builds not yet leased.

For Iron Mountain Incorporated: this is the clearest forward growth signal in the filings -- leasable MW roughly doubled from 250 (FY2023) to 488 (FY2025), and the pipeline under development (611 to 852 MW) is the revenue the Global Data Center segment is converting into over the next several years.

What to watch:

  • Under-development MW converting into leasable MW, not stalling
  • Lease-up pace and pre-leasing commitments disclosed alongside capacity
  • Capital intensity of the buildout versus the core records-management business

segmentRevenue.title: Segment revenue: Global RIM vs Global Data Center
segmentRevenue.content:
Iron Mountain reports two segments: Global RIM (physical records storage and information management, the legacy annuity business) and Global Data Center (colocation and hyperscale leasing, the growth business).

For Iron Mountain Incorporated: Global Data Center revenue grew from $495m (FY2023) to $803m (FY2025), roughly double Global RIM's growth rate off a much smaller base -- the segment mix shift is the thesis for the stock, not the stable but slow-growing RIM storage business alone.

What to watch:

  • Data Center's share of total revenue rising over time
  • RIM's organic growth holding up even as it becomes the smaller growth driver
  • Log scale here: the two segments differ by roughly 6-7x in size

storageRental.title: Storage rental revenue
storageRental.content:
Storage rental revenue is the recurring fee Iron Mountain earns simply for holding records and assets in its facilities -- as distinct from one-off service revenue (handling, destruction, project work).

For Iron Mountain Incorporated: this is the REIT-like annuity base the dividend is underwritten by; it grew from $3.37bn (FY2023) to $4.05bn (FY2025) with high retention and built-in price escalators.

What to watch:

  • Organic storage growth (volume and pricing) versus growth from acquisitions
  • Retention/churn in the underlying records base, disclosed qualitatively in filings

balanceSheet.title: Balance sheet
balanceSheet.content:
Shareholders' equity is assets less liabilities; plotted against total liabilities to show leverage.

For Iron Mountain Incorporated: equity that grows only through revaluations or share issues is not the same as retained earnings.

What to watch:

  • Liabilities growing faster than equity
  • Goodwill share of equity after acquisitions

cashDebt.title: Cash and debt
cashDebt.content:
Cash & equivalents against total borrowings (leases excluded unless noted).

For Iron Mountain Incorporated: the DCF's net-debt bridge uses these balances at the latest balance-sheet date.

What to watch:

  • Net debt trend versus EBITDA
  • Refinancing dates and covenants in the filings

ebitda.title: EBITDA
ebitda.content:
EBITDA is earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation -- an operating-cash proxy that ignores capital intensity.

For Iron Mountain Incorporated: read it beside CapEx: a business that must reinvest most of its EBITDA is not as cash-generative as the margin suggests.

What to watch:

  • EBITDA margin trend
  • Gap between EBITDA and operating cash flow (working capital)

epsDps.title: EPS and dividends
epsDps.content:
EPS is net income per share; DPS is the cash dividend paid per share. Both are in major currency units.

For Iron Mountain Incorporated: the payout ratio (DPS / EPS) shows how much of earnings is returned versus reinvested.

What to watch:

  • EPS growth versus net income growth (dilution)
  • Dividends funded from earnings, not debt

fcf.title: Free cash flow
fcf.content:
Reported FCF is operating cash flow less capital expenditure. Owner FCF (from the DCF) further deducts stock-based compensation, interest income and lease principal -- the cash an owner could actually take out.

For Iron Mountain Incorporated: the gap between net income and owner FCF is the earnings-quality question the valuation is built on.

What to watch:

  • FCF persistently below net income
  • Working-capital swings inflating one year's FCF

margins.title: Margins
margins.content:
Gross margin is revenue less cost of revenue; operating margin deducts operating expenses; net margin is after interest and tax.

For Iron Mountain Incorporated: the spread between gross and operating margin is the cost of running the business; a widening spread with flat gross margin means opex is growing faster than sales.

What to watch:

  • Direction of operating margin over several years, not one
  • One-offs (impairments, disposals) that distort net margin

ocfCapex.title: Operating cash flow and CapEx
ocfCapex.content:
Operating cash flow is cash generated by operations; CapEx is cash invested in fixed and intangible assets.

For Iron Mountain Incorporated: CapEx here is shown as stored (sign convention varies by ticker); the DCF splits it into stay-in-business and growth where disclosed.

What to watch:

  • CapEx rising faster than revenue
  • OCF that diverges from EBITDA

profit.title: Profit lines
profit.content:
Gross profit is revenue less cost of revenue; operating income deducts operating expenses; net income is after interest, tax and one-offs.

For Iron Mountain Incorporated: the three lines together show where margin is made and lost between the top line and the bottom.

What to watch:

  • Operating income growing slower than gross profit (opex creep)
  • Net income far from operating income (interest, tax, one-offs)

revenue.title: Revenue
revenue.content:
Revenue is the top line: what customers paid for goods and services in the period, before any costs.

For Iron Mountain Incorporated: the growth rate matters more than the level; compare it with the DCF's base-case growth path below.

What to watch:

  • Acceleration or deceleration in YoY growth
  • Whether growth is organic or acquired
  • Interim rows show seasonality

sbc.title: Stock-based compensation and share count
sbc.content:
Stock-based comp is the expense of equity awards; shares outstanding shows the dilution it causes net of buybacks.

For Iron Mountain Incorporated: the DCF charges SBC as a cash cost and holds the share count flat, so this chart is the check on that assumption.

What to watch:

  • Share count rising while buybacks are advertised
  • SBC as a percentage of revenue
